summary: Aluxes (singular alux, plural aluxo'ob) are small, mostly unseen guardian spirits of the milpa, the monte (bush), ancient mounds and ruins in Yucatec Maya folklore. The consistent, well-sourced core is: child-sized man-like beings in farmer's clothes and hat; they guard the field at night by whistling and throwing little stones at thieves; farmers ask their permission and give offerings (corn drink saka', food) before planting; if people forget, the aluxes play pranks (hide tools, rock hammocks, throw pebbles) and in stronger versions cause illness. A family-friendly beginner story is well supported. The 'little house' for the alux is real but versions differ (small house, hill, rock, field corner), and 'sak lool' appears in none of the sources - use saka' for the offering drink and 'kahtal alux' only if a house name is wanted.
facts: Aluxes are small beings of Yucatec Maya cosmology whose main job is to guard the milpa (cornfield) and other cultivated plots, and house plots, from thieves and intruders. Belief in them is still alive in Yucatan, strongest among people who work in the monte. [Villanueva 2014; Storniolo, Penn Museum Expedition; Wikipedia]

Size and look: described as child-sized (about like a 3-4 year old, or knee-high, up to roughly half a metre or a metre in other accounts) but with the face and manner of a small adult or old man; often bearded and wearing a hat. Height varies by account. [Villanueva 2014 citing Smailus 1976; Storniolo; Infobae; Wikipedia]

Dress and gear: they dress like Maya farmers - hat, alpargatas (sandals), and tools such as machete, coa or axe, plus a slingshot (tirahule) - and are often accompanied by a dog. [Villanueva 2014 citing Villa Rojas 1995; Words Without Borders (Dominguez Ake) gives the clay figure its own clay dog and slingshot]

They are mostly invisible. Farmers think of them as wind/spirit (ik') and know them by sounds: piercing whistling, objects dropping, pebbles thrown at intruders, sometimes shadows and tiny footprints. [Villanueva 2014; Storniolo]

Where they live: the monte around the milpa, small hills near the fields, ancient mounds and ruins (where they guard old tombs), caves and cenotes. Some people believe small ancient stone houses were their homes. [Storniolo; Villanueva 2014; Mexico News Daily; Infobae citing INPI]

How they guard: they frighten thieves by whistling and throwing stones, can make an intruder lose the way, and in one account the thief hears an unseen dog bark and flees. [Words Without Borders; Villanueva 2014; Storniolo]

How they help: they watch the field at night, scare animals and thieves, help the crop produce, and in dry spells can make the rain god chaac water the plot they guard. [Villanueva 2014 citing Villa Rojas; Storniolo; Infobae; Wikipedia]

The relationship is reciprocal: farmers ask permission with ritual and offerings before opening the monte for a milpa, thank the owners of the monte after harvest, and include the aluxes in those offerings. If farmers do not give the offerings, the aluxes stop doing their guarding work and cause trouble. [Villanueva 2014 citing Redfield 1944 and Boccara 2004]

Offerings named in sources: saka' (a corn drink, in one account with honey) given at the start of the work; saka' and k'ool (a thick broth) given yearly with prayers, led by a ritual specialist (h-men); corn atole; food and drink left at the hills; first-fruits (primicias) at Chichen Itza; sweets or fruit at small house shrines. [Words Without Borders; Villanueva 2014 (Tepich Carrillo); Por Esto 2022; Storniolo; Yucatan Today]
The h-men also names the people who live and work on the plot during the ritual so the aluxes know them from strangers and do not harm them. [Villanueva 2014, Tepich Carrillo fieldwork]

If ignored: mischief first - throwing pebbles, hiding or stealing tools, rocking hammocks at night, noises and screeching to get attention. Stronger versions say persistent neglect brings illness ('aires malos', bad winds). [Villanueva 2014; Storniolo; Words Without Borders]

If respected: the alux protects crops from animals and thieves and the owner and family are left alone; in one informant's story, after an h-men did the rites and offerings, peace returned to a troubled house; in the Words Without Borders account, giving saka' calms an alux. [Storniolo; Villanueva 2014; Words Without Borders]

Two main explanations of what an alux is: (1) a figure made by an h-men (clay in most accounts) and given life by ritual, then set to guard a plot; (2) the spirit of the first, ancient people of the land (builders of the mounds). Many people mix both. [Villanueva 2014; Storniolo; Words Without Borders]

The little house: several sources say the alux is tied to a small house built by the farmer in the milpa or at a special spot in it (Wikipedia; Na'atik; Por Esto 2022 and 2026). Small doll-sized house shrines for aluxes are also seen across the peninsula, including at construction sites and in towns; they are called kahtal alux, 'houses of the alux'. [Wikipedia; Na'atik; Yucatan Today; Sunset World page]

Modern life: Chichen Itza workers in 2008-2010 explained odd noises and a stage collapse by saying the aluxes had not been properly respected, and ceremonies are held at some construction sites. [Villanueva 2014 citing Diario de Yucatan; Mexico News Daily; Wikipedia]

In the Words Without Borders text (translated from Yucatec Maya, from a 1993 Maya-language collection), the aluxes are described as nocturnal, and someone who sees one alone should wait a few days before telling anyone, or may fall ill. [Words Without Borders]
variants: Origin: made by an h-men from clay (WWB, Villanueva, Por Esto 2026), from wax (Por Esto 2022) or from wood (Villanueva); OR spirits of the first/ancient inhabitants (Villanueva, Storniolo); OR made by the gods from mud, leaves and divine breath (Wikipedia); OR left incomplete by the gods (INALI via Infobae). Consistent core: small guardian beings of the monte and milpa.

Where the figure sits: in the middle of the field under a rock (Words Without Borders); at the corners of the plot (Villanueva); in a small palm-roofed house or a special spot in the milpa (Por Esto 2022, 2026); in small hills near the fields (Storniolo); in ancient mounds (Villanueva).

The seven-year rule: Wikipedia, Na'atik and popular pages say the alux helps for seven years, then the farmer seals the little house's doors and windows so it stays inside; if not, it runs wild and pranks people. No academic source read here confirms this. In the Words Without Borders account the farmer instead breaks the alux at the end of the work. Treat the seven-year sealing as one version only.

How the alux is brought to life: blood is given in several accounts (Villanueva, WWB, Por Esto); Villanueva citing Boccara says saka' replaces the blood and keeps the aluxes alive; Words Without Borders gives saka' thirteen times; Por Esto 2026 starts seven weeks before Good Friday. Details differ a lot.

Offering contents differ by village and writer: saka', k'ool, atole, food, fruit and sweets; Storniolo also lists alcohol and cigarettes; Wikipedia lists food, cigarettes, honey, corn. The shared core is food and a corn drink offered with respect and permission.

Height and look: 'like a 3-4 year old with an old face' (Villanueva), 'knee-high' (Wikipedia), about 40 cm (a Por Esto witness), about 1 m in elegant white jarana clothes (one Tepich Carrillo informant), 'color of clay' (Chan Kom farmer via Storniolo). Children in one study imagine them fat or thin, pale or even TV-style creatures.

Character: mischievous but helpful guardians (most sources); stricter and punishing if neglected (Villanueva, Por Esto); a few sources stress childlike playful pranks even in empty or inhabited houses (Villanueva).

Names by region: aluxo'ob in eastern Yucatan, Quintana Roo and Chenes (Campeche); kanan koolo'ob ('guardians of the milpa') in the Camino Real zone of Campeche (reported from a UNAM Instituto de Investigaciones Historicas chapter via search summary, not read directly). Spanish speakers also say duendes.

a thick broth/gravy-like ritual soup offered together with saka' (Villanueva 2014)

wind and vital force; the aluxes are thought of as ik'oob, which is why they are heard rather than seen
the Maya rain god; in one belief the aluxes can make a chaac water their field in a drought

cautions: The term 'sak lool' (in the brief) does not appear in any source found. Do not use it. The drink offered to aluxes is saka' (saka/zaca/sacab); a house is called kahtal alux in two non-academic sources only.

Blood: many ritual accounts (Words Without Borders, Villanueva, Por Esto) say the alux is given life with the owner's or h-men's blood. Leave this out of a children's/beginner story. Also leave out alcohol and cigarettes (mentioned by Storniolo and Wikipedia).

Death and ancestors: some sources link aluxes to ancestors or say they guard ancient tombs (Storniolo), and the h-men rites touch Catholic and Maya religion. Keep it simple and non-religious in the story, or hedge with 'people say' and avoid claiming what the Maya believe about the dead.

Present as living belief and storytelling, not as a mistaken superstition and not as proven fact. Use 'se dice / dicen / la gente cuenta' (it is said). Villages differ and some adults do not believe in aluxes (Villanueva 2014), so do not say 'all Maya believe'.

Do not state the seven-year sealing, the 13 saka' offerings, the 7 weeks before Good Friday, or the 'do not say their name' rule as general fact; each comes from one or two weak or popular sources and conflicts with other versions.

Avoid scary details: sealing the alux inside, smashing the alux at noon, punishment by illness, being lost among thorns (Por Esto 2022), or 'do not tell anyone you saw one or you get sick' (Words Without Borders). A light version (pebbles, whistle, hidden tools, rocked hammock) is the safe, consistent core.

Avoid tourist legends and viral items: the Cancun bridge/Kukulcan Boulevard shrines, the Elton John stage collapse, and the 2023 presidential photo are news/tourism stories, not folklore sources. Wikipedia itself notes weak evidence for pre-Columbian aluxes and a disputed pirate-influence theory; skip both.

Sources are uneven: only Villanueva 2014 (peer-reviewed, Universidad Autonoma de Yucatan) and Storniolo (Penn Museum) are scholarly; Words Without Borders is a translated Maya-language account; the rest are journalism, tourism or encyclopedia pages. kanan koolo'ob was reported through a search summary of a UNAM chapter and was not read directly.

Spelling varies (aluxo'ob / aluxob / aluxes; h-men / j-men / X'men / Ah men; saka' / saká / zacá / sacab). Pick one form and use it consistently; plural 'aluxes' is common in Spanish, aluxo'ob is the Maya plural.

Not to be confused with Nahuatl chaneques (Wikipedia notes the comparison) or with the pu'uses/zayan uinico'b dwarfs, which milperos in Tahmek keep distinct from aluxes. The Yucatec rain god Chaac is separate from the aluxes.
